## Overview

## 1.1 Context and Scope

The year 2026 constitutes a watershed moment in the governance of Level-4 (L4) autonomous trucking, marked by two parallel but philosophically divergent legislative trajectories on either side of the Atlantic. In the European Union, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) adopted a global regulatory framework for L4 automated driving systems (ADS) on 24 June 2026, establishing the first internationally harmonized technical type-approval regime for vehicles capable of sustained, driverless operation [2]. Concurrently, the United States federal surface transportation bill introduced a provision to create a national regulatory framework for autonomous commercial motor vehicles, a legislative breakthrough aimed at supplanting the current state-level patchwork with a unified Department of Transportation (DOT) oversight regime [24]. This Overview section delineates the architectural contours of these two regulatory breakthroughs, contrasts their operational implications for interstate highway deployment, and — critically — identifies the evidentiary boundaries of the available source materials with respect to adoption rates, insurance liability frameworks, and job displacement metrics. The analysis reveals that while both jurisdictions have made significant legislative progress on technical safety and type-approval, neither framework, as documented, contains binding provisions addressing the socio-economic externalities of L4 truck deployment.
